cards.title: FAA issues national ground stop – lifted 4.5 hours later

cards.title: Live airband on all frequencies from KORS. Victoria, CA also ground stopped

depth.text: someone built a **live airband feed** that transcribes **radio chatter** and summarizes what's happening in nearby airspace

At KORS, the setup uses an **ETTUS B210** and **cuda code on a GPU** to split the whole airband into channels, detect transmissions, and send them to a voice model for transcription; a separate LLM builds a picture of the airspace. The creator says the project grew from a pilot around KORS losing an engine in a 172 and putting it in the water; the community only heard about it days later. They hope to **open-source** the system so others can run stations.

cards.title: After 600 experiments, here's what I discovered about JEPA world models

One method chains **25-step subgoals**; another adds a cost to jumps between demonstrations in a memory graph. Together, those first two changes raised long-horizon success from **22% to 85%**.

long-horizon success after the first two methods

cards.camps: Two camps: some commenters found the transformed-memory idea interesting; others said the planning ideas were already well understood or that the tests mostly replayed demonstration data.

cards.title: Ukraine knocks out 36% of Russia's oil refining capacity in under two weeks

cards.title: Jonathan Blow – If AI solved coding, why is my software still the same? [video]

cards.camps: Some say AI mostly speeds up coding without changing what organizations build; others say it has made personal software and small projects much easier to create.

comments.text: It's because the hard part of making software is not coding, but deciding what's worth building (even with LLMs), appropriately modelling the problem and designing the solution (at a conceptual, architectural level). And there has been strictly zero progress on this and IMO this isn't something LLMs are strucurally capable of doing.

Blow argues software development hasn't advanced much since the early 2000s. As a game developer, I want to offer a counter point. In the last 3 years, there have been a lot more indie games of far higher quality than we used to get. I'm thinking of the RTS space right now. The Scouring for example. We went from having nobody but Blizzard able to make something that complex to several games with…
Because AI coding has only worked well in the last six months. Two years ago it sucked. A year ago it was flaky. Now, Claude nails a lot of problems routinely. What will next year bring?

AI hasn’t solved coding, if anything it’s made code quality worse. But it’s made it the process of coding faster. The latter is why managers love AI - and the former is why the general public hates it.

The video does actually answer its own title, which is refreshing. And I agree, it’s because organizations and people haven’t changed (yet, if you’re being positive) what it is they’re optimizing for and how they do work. AI gives you more of what you want and gives it faster, that doesn’t on its own change the culture or goals of a company.

cards.title: A technical vision for the Haskell ecosystem

depth.text: Haskell's **technical leaders** want to make it **easier to learn**, faster to build with, and more dependable

The Haskell Foundation’s technical leadership committee is now **operational** and wants companies, contractors, and volunteers to help develop and fund proposals. One concrete target is bringing GHC’s own CI turnaround from **6 hours to 2**; the vision also calls for friendlier onboarding, better debugging, stronger security, and long-term stability.

cards.camps: Two camps: some argue Haskell’s strictness and types could make it a strong fit for AI coding; others say it still lacks a compelling practical advantage and broader adoption compared with alternatives.

cards.title: No AI Slop: A Manifesto

cards.title: Terminal borders that don't cost a cell

depth.text: someone designed **terminal borders** that sit between cells without taking up **a row or column**

The protocol stores borders as a **cell attribute**, with each segment able to have its own color, width, placement and style. They aren't text, so selections don't copy them; the author has a working **Ghostty patch**.

cards.camps: Two camps: supporters like the new border capability; skeptics prefer simple text-first TUIs and worry about compatibility or terminals becoming GUIs.

comments.text: A much better alternative to this would be to for more terminal emulators to implement overstrike mode (DECSET 20, as available on the VK100). I love this work and everything else Ratatui does but I have to ask: if you're changing the terminal protocol and the terminal itself to do this, why not do something more ambitious; a full monospaced information-dense UI framework, a terminal designed for user interfaces, rather than one designed to replicate the limitations of dumb terminals?

I don't generally like TUI's and think one gets more flexibility with raw text interfaces and being able to glue things together is more important then them looking nice. I think less fancy out put is better to be honest.

cards.title: Nvidia director sold nearly $1B in stock weeks before the Jensen Huang scandal

Board director Mark Stevens sold about **$946 million** across three batches, without a **prearranged trading plan**. He still held **27.5 million shares**; the article says not having a plan isn't necessarily a red flag on its own.

cards.title: Found: A protein that drives ageing without unleashing inflammation

depth.text: researchers found a **protein** that drives ageing in mice without unleashing **inflammation**

The protein is **granzyme K**. Aged mice engineered to lack it had **improved heart and liver function** and **less kidney damage**. The abstract says it drives ageing in tissues, but not immune ageing or systemic inflammaging.

comments.text: Paper: https://www.cell.com/immunity/fulltext/S1074-7613(26)00440-1 Granzyme K is the protein.

From the abstract of the paper, significantly more nuance. > Despite persistent immune aging phenotypes, GzmK deficiency markedly attenuated organ aging, effectively uncoupling immune and tissue aging... These findings identify GzmK as a tissue-specific driver of organismal aging but not immune aging or systemic inflammaging.
Paywall
In mice.
Thank God! Finally, mice that don't age!

cards.title: Brazil's Caixa insurer breach exposes names and tax IDs of all 7.6M customers

depth.text: a breach at Brazil's Caixa insurer exposed **names and tax IDs** for **all 7.6M customers**

Several commenters say **CPFs are already widely exposed**, but names paired with phone numbers and Caixa customer clues could **help scammers pose as the bank**. One commenter doubts the claim that no financial data was exposed.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say CPF-only leaks are old news because the number is widely shared; others worry customer details make fraud easier and question whether financial data was really safe.

comments.text: No financial information leaked, just tax id, which in Brazil nowadays doesn't mean much. There have been more than one high profile website in the past reportedly selling personal data, including tax identifier (CPF), for essentially any Brazilian citizen. It is common to be asked for your CPF for trivial things like purchasing anything on a drugstore, and for any and all activity with…

I'm pretty sure at this point every tax ID (CPF) in Brazil is available on a database you can get on the dark web. We've had a "CPF-ication" of everything in Brazil over the last few years. The vast majority of people have shared this number with their local grocery store, pharmacy, gym, etc. It's required for a lot of stuff and pretty necessary for others. Given that, if that's all that leaked…

For those who don't know it, our tax id (CPF) is basically public information. For instance: we just had an election. The official public site with the official information about all the candidates ( https://divulgacandcontas.tse.jus.br/ ) has the CPF for all of them. Want to know our president's CPF? It's there. The bad part is the rest. Having the name together with the phone number, plus being…
It's important to note the Brazilian tax id (CPF) is not meant to be a well kept secret like the American SSN

Small potatoes. CPFs have been leaked so many times in Brazil that probably all of them are already out there. [0][1][2] [0] https://cyberbrics.info/the-largest-personal-data-leakage-in... cards.title: Ggml v1.0.0

depth.text: someone gave a machine-learning library a **major update**, with **performance work** across several hardware backends

Version 1.0.0 prunes the deprecated public API, adds YaRN truncation and **OCP FP8 support**, and brings performance work across CUDA/Metal, Vulkan, SYCL, OpenCL, and WebGPU. Highlights include **few-row quantized matmuls** and a **device-side MoE scheduler**.

comments.text: What is really impressive about this project and llama.cpp as well is that they keep finding new ways to speed up the code on the same hardware. Every time I upgrade (once a month or so) there is usually a 5 to 10% speed boost. edit: Just to verify: I had planned to upgrade today, ran my usual benchmark prior and after and the runtime went from 4:22 to 3:59. That's a really long prompt (50K…

Awesome! ggml and llama.cpp are the Linux of the AI world. Driving local inference one bit at a time. Wishing you unlimited power and may you never see a day of low battery. Respect and Love. Keep it up.
Long time llama.cpp user (and user of other ggml based AI programs) running on my crappy AMD card that only supports vulkan and it's usable thanks to GGML and llama.cpp, great program great project.
I prefer this entry point: https://github.com/ggml-org/ggml

In my opinion, this is a genuine engineering product.
LLM.cpp, the savior of our difficult times...

cards.title: Minnesota guitarist's "palmfrets" invention strikes a new chord

depth.text: a Minnesota guitarist's **palmfrets** let players raise **bass-string notes** with their palm near the bridge

A commenter describes it as a **fret at the bridge end**, which raises the bass strings' root note by a semitone or few. Another says it can make you **your own bass backing player** with one or two notes.

cards.camps: Two camps: some see new musical possibilities or a useful bass part; others say it adds little, could feel awkward, or can be replaced by alternate tuning.

cards.title: OpenAI disbands its robotics team as its general models start running robots

depth.text: OpenAI disbanded its **robotics team** as its **general AI models** start controlling robots

Robotics researchers moved to the **main research team** under Mark Chen, while applied robotics and hardware went to the larger Applied organization under Greg Brockman. In an Nvidia study, an Astra-powered agent scored **74.8%** on a simulated robotics test, compared with **51.0%** for the best specialized robotic models on that leaderboard.
data: Astra-powered agent success rate on a simulated manipulation benchmark
Best specialized robotic models’ reported success rate on the leaderboard

cards.camps: Two camps: general-model optimists say broad AI can handle robotics; skeptics say robots still need faster specialized models and real-world experience.

comments.text: General models can run robots. They are very bad at it. It is much more efficient to have a stack of models with 'dumber' but faster models taking care of lower level functions and higher level ones that are much slower taking care of high level planning. Consciousness isn't super fast, but it is very smart. Your 'lizard brain' (to use an overstretched metaphor) and reflexive system are…
The Bitter Lesson comes for everything.
This looks like general cost cutting to boost some numbers before IPO.
So they gave up on non-cloud connected robotics then? Or was that ever in their scope?
Is there a primer on how to actually use LLMs to control robots? Seems very token inefficient if you have to stream commands at 60fps.

cards.title: Amtrak booking system experiencing major issues amid nationwide FAA ground stop

depth.text: Amtrak's **booking system** went down during a nationwide FAA ground stop, then began **returning to normal**

Travelers showed **error messages** on Amtrak's website and app; officials said the issues were related to a **system-wide update**, but did not elaborate. Around 9 p.m., the booking systems were **returning to normal**, though some customers could still have issues processing payments, booking trips, or modifying reservations.

cards.title: Microsoft outage gives customers a crash course in dependence on Redmond

depth.text: a **Microsoft outage** left **email gone and Teams iffy**, showing organizations' reliance on **one provider**

Microsoft put the incident's start at **1826 GMT on November 12**. **Exchange Online**, recently used files in Microsoft 365, Copilot and Microsoft 365 Education were affected; on November 13, Microsoft said availability was improving. Nextcloud co-founder Jos Poortvliet said companies may struggle to switch providers quickly or keep working **air-gapped**.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say a day out every few years isn't worth paying more to avoid; others say a business taken offline by its SaaS isn't resilient.

comments.text: I wonder if it'll be a more useful course than the one we had when Crowdstrike broke everything, or the many times when AWS US-East-1 has fallen over taking down many popular services. The lesson most people learn from this sort of outage is that things bounce back afterwards, and the risk is minimal enough that a day out of every few years isn't enough of a problem to pay more.

I think every N days a chaos monkey event should happen for every business to help with this kind of issue. If a SaaS takes your business offline, you aren't resilient. https://netflix.github.io/chaosmonkey/

That ship sailed 20 years ago when everybody stampeded into cloud computing / SaaS ago and it became heresy to suggest on-prem had benefits. "Redmond" is a symptom but the problem is "live by the cloud, die by the cloud."

Microsoft Ireland Operations Limited is designated as a DORA 3TPP [1]... I wonder if that corporate entity is in-scope to pay penalties for this outage. ---
[1] https://www.regulation-dora.eu/blog/critical-ict-third-party...
